items.en: Resolving Points about Dharma and Mind
parent: V. Discriminating the Dharma and Mind of Dhyāna-Pāramitā

zh:
第三、料簡法心。問曰：諸佛說一切法皆空，絕諸言句。如《摩訶衍論》偈說：「般若波羅蜜，譬如大火焰，四邊不可取，邪見火燒故。」今云何作四句分別，將非墮戲論乎？答曰：佛法中不可得空，於諸法無所礙，因是不可得空故，說一切佛法十二部經。今說有四句無咎。譬如虛空，雖無所有，而一切物依以長成。如《摩訶衍論》偈說：
若信諸法空，是則順於理；
若不信法空，一切皆違失。
若以無是空，無所應造作。
未作已有業，不作有作者。
如是諸法相，誰能思量者？
唯有得直心，所說無依止，
離於有無見，心自然內滅。
en: Third, resolving points about dharma and mind. Question: The buddhas teach that all dharmas are empty, cutting off every word and phrase — as the Mahāyāna treatise says in verse: "The perfection of wisdom is like a great blazing flame; it cannot be grasped from any of its four sides, since wrong views are burned away by it." Why, then, is a fourfold scheme now being set forth — is this not falling into idle theorizing?

Answer: Within the Buddhadharma, the emptiness that cannot be grasped is precisely what places no obstruction on any dharma whatsoever — it is because of this ungraspable emptiness that the whole Buddhadharma, the twelve divisions of scripture, can be spoken at all. There is no fault, then, in now speaking of a fourfold scheme. It is like empty space itself: though it possesses nothing at all, every single thing depends on it in order to grow and take form. As the Mahāyāna treatise says in verse:
"If one has faith that all dharmas are empty, this accords with principle;
If one lacks faith in the emptiness of dharmas, everything goes astray.
If, taking this 'nothing' to be emptiness, one concludes there is nothing to be done at all —
Then karma already exists before any action, and there is one who acts even without acting.
Such being the marks of all dharmas, who is there that could ever fully fathom them?
Only one who has attained a straightforward mind, whose every word rests on nothing at all,
Free of the views of existence and nonexistence, whose mind is naturally extinguished from within."

zh: 今為開發行人方便知見，分別種種法門，故無句義中辨於句義，於理無失，故《大品經》云：「無句義是菩薩句義。」若汝欲離四句求解脫者，即還被無句縛。所以然者，如說有四句、無四句、亦有四句亦無四句、非有四句非無四句，汝尚不免無四句縛，豈得免亦有亦無等四句縛？當知了句非句，於句義無礙而得解脫，非是離句求於無句而得解脫，如天女呵身子云：「無離文字說解脫也。文字性離即解脫相。」
en: Here, in order to open up skillful understanding and insight for practitioners, the various dharma-gates are distinguished — hence, within what is without any conceptual content, conceptual content is nonetheless discerned, and this involves no fault in principle. Hence the Larger Sūtra says: "What is without conceptual content is itself the bodhisattva's own conceptual content." If you wish to seek liberation by leaving the fourfold scheme behind, you will only be bound instead by "no fourfold scheme." Why is this? For if one speaks of "having the fourfold scheme," "lacking the fourfold scheme," "both having and lacking it," or "neither having nor lacking it" — if you cannot even escape being bound by "lacking the fourfold scheme," how could you escape being bound by "both having and lacking" or the rest? One should know that liberation is attained by understanding that a concept is not fixed as a concept, remaining unobstructed within conceptual content itself — not by leaving concepts behind to seek some concept-free state and thereby attaining liberation. As the heavenly maiden rebuked Śāriputra, saying: "There is no such thing as speaking of liberation apart from the written word. The very nature of the written word being itself free of fixed self-nature is precisely the mark of liberation."

zh:
復次，今明法之與心合為八句，迴轉分別則有三十六句。若細歷法而明，即出無量句。若能於一句法通達一切句，則此辨若虛空，無有邊際。問曰：若爾，何以不約法心各作五句？答曰：諸佛出世，對緣化物，教門多約四句，如《摩訶衍論》中說，有四種悉檀：一、世界悉檀；二、為人悉檀；三、對治悉檀；四、第一義悉檀。初、有漏法心即是世界悉檀攝；二、無漏法心即是對治悉檀攝；三、亦有漏亦無漏法心即是為人悉檀攝；四、非有漏非無漏法心即是第一義悉檀攝。是中相攝之意，細尋可見。復次，《摩訶衍論》又於第一義悉檀中分別四門，如論偈說：
一切實一切不實，一切亦實亦不實，
一切非實非非實，如是皆名諸法實。
如是等，但有四句，更無第五句。今約四句明法心可以類此。餘經論中設有五句明義別有因緣，今取一途義便，故不約五句分別。
en: Furthermore: dharma and mind, taken together here, make eight statements; turned and distinguished further, they make thirty-six. If one traces through every dharma in fine detail, measureless statements emerge. And if one can, through a single statement about a single dharma, penetrate every statement whatsoever, then this analysis is as boundless as empty space itself.

Question: If this is so, why not sort dharma and mind each into five statements instead? Answer: When the buddhas appear in the world, teaching according to the occasion to transform beings, the gate of teaching is, for the most part, arranged around a fourfold scheme — as the Mahāyāna treatise explains, there are four kinds of siddhānta: first, the worldly siddhānta; second, the siddhānta for the individual; third, the siddhānta of the antidote; fourth, the siddhānta of ultimate meaning. Contaminated dharma-mind belongs to the worldly siddhānta; uncontaminated dharma-mind belongs to the siddhānta of the antidote; both contaminated and uncontaminated dharma-mind belongs to the siddhānta for the individual; neither contaminated nor uncontaminated dharma-mind belongs to the siddhānta of ultimate meaning. The sense in which each corresponds to the other can be seen by tracing it through in detail.

Furthermore, the Mahāyāna treatise, within the siddhānta of ultimate meaning itself, further distinguishes four approaches, as the treatise says in verse:
"Everything is real, everything is unreal,
Everything is both real and unreal,
Everything is neither real nor unreal —
All of these alike are called the true reality of all dharmas."
Statements of this kind number only four, with never a fifth. The present fourfold clarification of dharma and mind may be understood along the same lines. Where other sūtras and treatises do set forth a fivefold scheme for their own purposes, that has its own separate rationale; here, for the sake of a single, convenient approach, a fivefold division is not adopted.

This is the treatise's first sustained excursion into explicit Madhyamaka-style argument, and it earns its place here by answering a real objection: if everything is empty and beyond words, doesn't a treatise this elaborate — ten topics, endless named lists, a fourfold scheme applied to everything — betray the very teaching it claims to serve? Zhiyi's answer is that emptiness is not a reason to stop speaking, but the very thing that makes speech possible without fixing anything in place, "like empty space itself... [which] everything depends on... in order to grow and take form." The four kinds of siddhānta (四悉檀) named here — worldly, for-the-individual, antidotal, and ultimate — are Nāgārjuna's own framework for why the Buddha teaches the same truth differently depending on the audience and occasion; matching each of the four dharma-mind categories to one siddhānta each is Zhiyi's own addition.

quiz.q: The four kinds of dharma-mind are matched to the four siddhāntas. Which siddhānta does "both contaminated and uncontaminated dharma-mind" belong to?
quiz.why: Contaminated belongs to the worldly; "uncontaminated dharma-mind belongs to the siddhānta of the antidote; both contaminated and uncontaminated dharma-mind belongs to the siddhānta for the individual"; neither belongs to ultimate meaning. Note the cross-over: uncontaminated pairs with the third-listed siddhānta, "both" with the second.
